```{r, include=FALSE}
library(highcharter)
hc_set_theme("hcrt", tooltip = list(valueDecimals = 2))
```

## Introduction

We chart data, and data can come in different ways: numeric or character vectors,
as time series objects, etc. but the most common object with data is a data 
frame. So, we'll show how  chart this type of object in __highcharter__.

Highcharter have two main functions to create a chart from data and another
to add data to an existing `highchart` object.

1. `hchart()`: A generic function which take an object (like vector, time series,
data frames, likert object, etc) and return a `highchart` object (chart)
2. `hc_add_series()`: A generic function which add data to a existing
`highchart` object depending the type (class) of the data.

There are a last function will be useful to chart data from data frame. The 
functions is `hcaes` which will define the aesthetic mappings. This 3 functions
are inspired in __ggplot2__ package. So:

- `hchart()` works like ggplot2's `qplot`.
- `hc_add_series()` works like ggplot2's `geom_`s.
- `hcaes()` works like ggplot2's `aes`.

The main differences with ggplot2 are here we need the data and the aesthetics
explicit in every highcharts functions. 

First, show some data to work with.

```{r}
data("mpg", "diamonds", "economics_long", package = "ggplot2")
head(mpg)
```

In general we'll use this structure to get a chart:

```
hchart(<data.frame>, <type_of_chart>, hcaes(<aesthetics>), ...)
```

- `<data.frame>` will be the data to chart.
- `<type_of_chart>` is a string to specify the type of chart. This value can 
be: line, spline, area, heatmap, treemap, etc.
- `<aesthetics>` is the mapping to use for plot.
- `...` are other parameters to configure the chart.

So, a basic example would be:

```{r}
hchart(mpg, "point", hcaes(x = displ, y = cty, group = year))
```

## Map positions and values

Lines and scatter plots place each observation at `x` and `y`. Add `group` to
split observations into series, `size` to give scatter points a bubble size,
or `color` to color individual points. A heatmap uses `value` to color a cell.

```{r}
data(economics_long, package = "ggplot2")

economics_long2 <- dplyr::filter(economics_long, variable %in% c("pop", "uempmed", "unemploy"))

head(economics_long2)

hchart(economics_long2, "line", hcaes(x = date, y = value01, group = variable))
```

Now, a heatmap and a treemap.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

dfdiam <- diamonds |> 
  group_by(cut, clarity) |>
  summarize(price = median(price))

hchart(dfdiam, "heatmap", hcaes(x = cut, y = clarity, value = price), name = "Median Price") 

mpgman <- mpg |> 
  group_by(manufacturer) |> 
  summarise(n = n(),
            unique = length(unique(model))) |> 
  arrange(-n, -unique)

hchart(mpgman, "treemap", hcaes(x = manufacturer, value = n, color = unique))
```

## Map ranges and summaries

Use `low` and `high` for vertical bounds in an area range or error bar.
An X-range uses `x` and `x2` for the two ends of a horizontal interval.

### Task intervals

Each row spans two dates. Map the start to `x`, the end to `x2` and the lane's zero-based index to `y`.

```{r mapping-xrange}
tasks <- data.frame(
  start = as.Date(c("2025-01-06", "2025-01-08")),
  finish = as.Date(c("2025-01-09", "2025-01-13")),
  lane = 0:1
)
hchart(tasks, "xrange", hcaes(x = start, x2 = finish, y = lane)) |>
  hc_yAxis(categories = c("Design", "Review"))
```

### Five-number summaries

Each row supplies the two whisker ends, the lower and upper quartiles, and the median for one box.

```{r mapping-boxplot}
waits <- data.frame(
  clinic = c("North", "South"), lower = c(4, 6), p25 = c(6, 8),
  p50 = c(10, 12), p75 = c(14, 15), upper = c(19, 22)
)
hchart(waits, "boxplot",
  hcaes(x = clinic, low = lower, q1 = p25, median = p50, q3 = p75, high = upper))
```

## Map links between nodes

Each row describes a link. Map its two node IDs to `from` and `to`. The
series type determines what you can read from those links.

| What you want to show | Series | Point fields |
|---|---|---|
| Which nodes are connected | `networkgraph` | `from`, `to` |
| How much flows between them | `sankey`, `dependencywheel`, `arcdiagram` | `from`, `to`, `weight` |
| Who reports to whom | `organization` | `from` (parent), `to` (child) |

These trips connect two districts to two transport modes. In the Sankey
diagram, the width of each link shows how many passengers took that route.

```{r mapping-sankey}
trips <- data.frame(
  origin = c("North", "North", "South"), destination = c("Bus", "Rail", "Rail"),
  passengers = c(30, 20, 15)
)
hchart(trips, "sankey", hcaes(from = origin, to = destination, weight = passengers))
```

### Style network nodes and tooltips

Rail serves both districts. To show those connections, reuse the trip table
as the links of a `networkgraph`. Style the endpoints separately in `nodes`,
matching each `id` to a value in `from` or `to`. Here blue identifies districts
and orange identifies transport modes. Circle area is proportional to the
passenger total at each node.

```{r mapping-networkgraph}
passengers <- tapply(rep(trips$passengers, 2), c(trips$origin, trips$destination), sum)
nodes <- lapply(names(passengers), function(id) {
  n <- passengers[[id]]
  district <- id %in% trips$origin
  list(
    id = id, name = if (district) paste(id, "district") else id,
    color = if (district) "#386B9E" else "#BD6333",
    marker = list(radius = 2 * sqrt(n)),
    custom = list(passengers = n)
  )
})

hchart(trips, "networkgraph", hcaes(from = origin, to = destination),
       nodes = nodes,
       dataLabels = list(enabled = TRUE, format = "{point.name}", linkFormat = ""),
       tooltip = list(headerFormat = "",
                      nodeFormat = "<b>{point.name}</b><br>Passengers: {point.custom.passengers}"))
```

`dataLabels.format` shows the node name on the chart. `tooltip.nodeFormat`
adds detail on hover. Hover over Rail to see 35 passengers, 20 from North
and 15 from South.

If you already have an `igraph` object, `hchart(graph, layout = igraph::layout_with_fr)`
uses the layout calculated in R and carries node attributes into the chart.

## Map a vector field

Each row is a measurement at a grid position. `x` and `y` locate the arrow,
`length` gives its relative magnitude, and `direction` sets its angle in degrees.

```{r mapping-vector}
field <- expand.grid(east = 1:4, north = 1:3)
field$speed <- 2 + field$north
field$bearing <- 30 * (field$east - 1)

hchart(field, "vector", hcaes(east, north, length = speed, direction = bearing),
       name = "Current") |>
  hc_xAxis(min = 0.5, max = 4.5, tickInterval = 1) |>
  hc_yAxis(min = 0.5, max = 3.5, tickInterval = 1)
```

## Extra parameters

You can add other parameters to add options to the data series. This options
can modify the names of each series/group. These names are used in the legend
as well the tooltip. You can modify the colors and a lot of properties.

```{r}
mpgman2 <- count(mpg, manufacturer, year)

hchart(
  mpgman2, 
  "bar",
  hcaes(x = manufacturer, y = n, group = year),
  color = c("#7CB5EC", "#F7A35C"),
  name = c("Year 1999", "Year 2008"),
  showInLegend = c(TRUE, FALSE) # only show the first one in the legend
  )
```

Highcharts has a very complete API with a lot of options. You can 
see every option in action in https://api.highcharts.com/highcharts/plotOptions.series.

## A more advanced example

Fit a local regression and compute its predictions and standard errors:

```{r, message=FALSE}
modlss <- loess(dist ~ speed, data = cars)

prediction <- predict(modlss, se = TRUE)
fit <- mutate(cars, .fitted = prediction$fit, .se = prediction$se.fit) |>
  arrange(speed)

head(fit)
```

In this case we'll chart the original data first and store in a variable called
`hc` (for highcharts):

```{r}
hc <- hchart(
  cars,
  type = "scatter",
  hcaes(x = speed, y = dist),
  name = "Speed and Stopping Distances of Cars",
  showInLegend = TRUE
  )

hc
```

We can add more series to chart (like the layers in ggplot world) using the
function `hc_add_series`. The parameters in this functions are similar to
the `hchart`:


```r
hc_add_series(<highcarter_object>, <data.frame>, <type_of_chart>, hcaes(<aesthetics>), ...)

# or with the pipe:

<highcarter_object> |> hc_add_series(<data.frame>, <type_of_chart>, hcaes(<aesthetics>), ...)

```

In this case we will add 2 groups of series. The 1st to add will be the 
spline then the arearange. So we'll use `hc_add_series` 2 times.

```{r}
qtint <- qt(0.975, prediction$df)

hc |>
  hc_add_series(
    fit,
    type = "spline",
    hcaes(x = speed, y = .fitted),
    name = "Fit",
    id = "fit", # this is for link the arearange series to this one and have one legend
    lineWidth = 1,
    showInLegend = TRUE
    ) |> 
  hc_add_series(
    fit,
    type = "arearange",
    name = "SE",
    hcaes(x = speed, low = .fitted - qtint*.se, high = .fitted + qtint*.se),
    linkedTo = "fit", # here we link the legends in one.
    showInLegend = FALSE,
    color = hex_to_rgba("gray", 0.2),  # put a semi transparent color
    zIndex = -3 # this is for put the series in a back so the points are showed first
    )
```

Example of data from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/22717930/how-to-get-the-confidence-intervals-for-lowess-fit-using-r.
